items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories
items.summary: Meet Another Build File Service (ABFS), Google's open-source content-addressable filesystem and build cache that cuts Android checkouts to <8s and builds to ~2m.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
items.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

items.title: DevFest is back!
items.summary: DevFest 2026 runs from October 1 to December 31, bringing together nearly a million developers across more than 800 global events centered on the agentic AI era. Under the theme "Build, Secure, Scale," participants gain hands-on experience with Google’s developer stack—including Gemini, Google AI Studio, Google Antigravity, and Web MCP—through live workshops and codelabs. The conference focuses on enabling developers to prototype rapidly, ensure secure and private deployments, and leverage production-ready infrastructure.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Gemini 4 Hydrogen: a faster model for general purpose robotics
items.summary: Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen brings strong spatial and embodied reasoning capabilities to a fast, efficient model built specifically for robotics. To help developers put these capabilities to work, the new Robotics plugin for Google Antigravity transforms the platform into a comprehensive workbench supporting rapid hardware bring-up, MuJoCo simulation, and closed-loop control. Developers can leverage these tools to transition from an unboxed robot arm to a fully functional real-to-sim-to-real application in an afternoon using natural language prompts and day-one support in the google-genai SDKs.

items.title: Smaller apps and faster GPU inference with LiteRT in Google Play services
items.summary: LiteRT in Google Play services now offers GPU inference powered by ML Drift, delivering about 1.4x faster performance alongside the new CompiledModel API. Switching from bundled binaries reduces app size by approximately 8 MB while enabling seamless, automatic runtime updates across billions of devices. Developers can easily adopt these updates by updating their dependencies and utilizing the new Android Studio LiteRT skill for automated migration.

items.title: A2UI 1.0: Build delightful, fast, reliable, agentic experiences
items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. The release introduces bidirectional function calls, swappable inference formats, and secure data binding to help teams seamlessly integrate generative UI into their product stacks.

items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: TPU Model Design Considerations and Optimization Guide
items.summary: The newly launched AI-Hypercomputer/tpu-codesign guide provides hardware-grounded design rules to help developers maximize performance on TPUs for LLMs and Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) workloads. Key principles include aligning reduction and output dimensions to 256 for systolic arrays, adopting LatentMoE to compress routed token traffic, and mapping parallel axes directly onto physical links.

items.title: Unlocking Stable On-Policy RL on TPU with Bitwise-Zero Train–Inference Mismatch
items.summary: How we eliminated floating-point train–inference logprob drift for on-policy LLM reinforcement learning across 64 Cloud TPU v5p chips using a generalizable four-part JAX and Pallas recipe in Tunix.

items.title: Hill-Climbing Agent Quality with Agents CLI Evaluation
items.summary: This post walks through the Agents CLI evaluation loop for systematically improving agent performance through continuous testing and grading. It demonstrates how to catch prompt regressions, evaluate model backend swaps using side-by-side trace comparisons, and automate evaluation passes. Developers will also learn how to integrate nightly scheduled runs with threshold-based alerting to track quality over time.

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection (AAD) provides asynchronous, low-latency monitoring for AI agents by analyzing OpenTelemetry traces and logs to flag goal hijacks and tool misuse. Tested across five public security benchmarks, AAD successfully caught 87% of harmful instructions carried out by agents without adding runtime latency. Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

items.title: Securing Your Agents: A Hands-On Guide to Agent Anomaly Detection
items.summary: This guide walks developers through setting up Agent Anomaly Detection on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform to monitor AI agent telemetry and catch behavioral risks. It demonstrates how to deploy a sample customer support agent, trigger out-of-scope security findings, and configure proactive alerts using Cloud Monitoring and Security Command Center.

items.title: From prompt to app: Build with Google Maps in AI Studio
items.summary: Developers can now build applications powered by Google Maps Platform directly within Google AI Studio by prompting Gemini with real-world geospatial concepts. The integration eliminates traditional configuration hurdles by providing one-click demo keys that generate instantly without requiring Cloud Console redirects or credit cards. This setup grants developers immediate access to core APIs—including Maps, Places, and Routes—supported by daily sandbox quotas for seamless prototyping.

items.title: I built a sandbox to win a security test and Deno tied me
items.summary: I wanted a clean win. I got a tie, plus a number that makes my sandbox look bad if you read it the wrong way. Here is the setup. Vow is a programming language I built for AI agents to write. Every function declares whether it can touch the network, files or environment: uses net, uses fs, uses env. So before you run anything an agent wrote, you can read what it is allowed to reach. Nobody has to guess. Then vow --sandbox does the checking for you, before anything runs. If the program reaches past what you allow, it gets refused. $ vow --sandbox --allow fs=./data app.vow x SandboxError: needs capabilities the sandbox does not grant env: fn leak declares 'uses env' Nothing was run. I like that last line a lot. Nothing was run. The function called leak never gets a turn. I wrote 7 attack programs and judged them with canaries. If a canary gets touched, the attack worked. I ran Vow's sandbox against them, and I ran TypeScript under Deno against the same 7 as a comparison. The first run was on October 2, 2026. Vow blocked 6 of 7. That missing one was my fault. items.title: 5 Ways Node.js Logistics Thumbnail Pipelines Avoid Object Storage Upload Timeouts
items.summary: A thumbnail job should not make a customer wait for a large object-storage upload. For a logistics system, the least complex reliable choice is to upload the original first, record a pending thumbnail, and process the derivative asynchronously. The request finishes after the original is durably accepted; a worker owns resizing, retries, and status updates. That shape also protects the less visible workflow: every tenant may have backups, and an operator may need to restore one selected snapshot later. Keep the original and each derivative addressable by tenant, object id, and snapshot. Access control stays explicit while delivery stays simple. items.title: Japanese PII detection that never leaves the browser (Transformers.js + a small ONNX model)
items.summary: TL;DR — We released ja-pii-ner-v1, a 111M-parameter model that detects 18 types of PII in Japanese text and runs fully on-device via ONNX / Transformers.js. On a held-out test of 10,001 documents it scores span F1 0.9770, with zero false positives on 2,068 PII-free documents, at 224 ms per document on a desktop CPU. Trained and evaluated only on synthetic data. Apache 2.0. The scrubbing tool should not be another place your raw text leaks to. If you call a cloud API to remove personal data before sending text to an LLM, the unscrubbed text has already left your hands. Running the detector locally — in the browser, or on your own CPU — makes the scrubbing step itself private. Measured, not promised: span precision 0.9965 / recall 0.9582 / F1 0.9770 on the full test split (10,001 documents, 43,064 gold spans), and 0 false positives across 2,068 documents that contain no PII at all. The ONNX fp32 export reproduces the PyTorch model exactly on the full test set. The honest weak points are in the open: ORGANIZATION recall is 0.879 and SECRET recall is 0.800. items.title: Google indexed 30 of my 547 pages. Here's what was wrong with my React SPA.
items.summary: I run GAGPedia, a free fan-made calculator and guide site for the Roblox game Grow a Garden: trade (Win/Fair/Loss) checks, plant values with mutation multipliers, pet XP tools, a codes page and some strategy guides. It's a Vite + React + TypeScript single-page app on Vercel, with game data in Supabase. After eight months live, Search Console looked like this: 547 URLs in the sitemap, 30 indexed 508 "Discovered – currently not indexed" 39 clicks from Google in total Meanwhile Bing (plus Yahoo and DuckDuckGo, which use its index) was sending roughly ten times more search visits than Google. So the pages weren't broken. Google just didn't think most of them were worth indexing. Here's what I found and fixed, in order of impact. The site generated a page for every pet (372) and every plant (115). Each one came out of the same template: about 325 words, of which one or two sentences were actually unique (an XP rate, a rank, a tier). I diffed two pet pages and they were 80% identical word for word. items.title: Content Taxonomy 1.0 vs 2.2 vs 3.1: Mapping CSVs vs cattax on OpenRTB
items.summary: When the OpenRTB 2.6-202501 snapshot landed on 27 January 2025, AdCOM gained Content Taxonomy 3.1 (cattax: 9) and the content.gtax / content.genres pair for CTV genre metadata. Product teams read that as “finish the 3.x upgrade.” Operations teams read the IAB Content Taxonomy mappings page as “run the CSV from 1.0 to 2.0 to 2.2.” Both are real. Only one of them versions the integers on the live bid. OpenRTB does not ship a mapping file. It ships cat arrays and a per-object cattax selector. If your migration stops at the spreadsheet, every downstream hop still assumes Content Category Taxonomy 1.0 wherever cattax is missing. That is the comparison practitioners confuse: offline mapping tables versus the on-wire selector that names which table applies. Taxonomy 1.0 is the flat IAB content list AdCOM still labels cattax: 1. OpenRTB 2.6 text is explicit: when an object omits cattax, receivers assume 1.0 for the cat, pagecat, sectioncat, or blocklist arrays on that same object. 1.0 is deprecated for new labeling, but it is not dead on the wire. items.title: A Scientific Calculator Where 0.1 + 0.2 Is Exactly 0.3 — Built From Addition Alone
items.summary: In JavaScript or Python, 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004. I ran a few more expressions in Node.js and Python: Expression JavaScript / Python morc calculator 0.1 + 0.2 0.30000000000000004 = 0.3 0.1 * 3 0.30000000000000004 = 0.3 1.1 * 3 3.3000000000000003 = 3.3 10 / 3 * 3 10 (the intermediate 10/3 is 3.3333333333333335) = 10 10 / 3 * 3 comes back to 10 only because the rounding in the final multiplication happens to cancel the error. With floating point, whether an error shows up depends on the numbers, and you cannot tell in advance. This is not a bug. Most computers store numbers as binary floating point, and 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so it is slightly off from the start. That part is well known. I have been working on a framework I call B13, where every calculation is done with integers, addition, and comparison only. Using that toolkit, I built an everyday scientific calculator. Code: morc_mini_en.html on GitHub Calculator: https://codepen.io/morc_b13-bit/pen/01a1ede0-a27b-72f4-ac1c-672a0d815de0 It is one HTML file. Open it in any browser, on a PC or a phone. items.title: Building Resilient Web Applications: Beyond Offline Loading (Part 2)
items.summary: Making web applications useful when the backend is unavailable. In Part 1, we explored the challenges of building web applications for unreliable networks and low-bandwidth environments. We discussed bandwidth, latency, browser storage, Service Workers, the Cache API, and how to make an application's shell available offline. By the end, our Resilient Task Board could load its application shell after it had been installed and its required resources cached. But there was still a problem. The application could open offline, but could it actually do anything useful? Imagine opening a task management application without an internet connection. The interface loads successfully, but your tasks are missing because the application still depends on an API request to retrieve them. You try creating a task, and the request fails because the backend is unreachable. We have improved availability, but we haven't solved data availability or offline interaction. This is where the next layer of resilience begins. An application can be available without its data being available. items.title: Rate Limiting in Vineforce Teams: Designing Dynamic API Policies on ASP.NET Core
items.summary: Overview Vineforce Teams is built on ASP.NET Zero, and it inherits ASP.NET Zero's dynamic rate limiting feature. Rate limiting policies are not hard-coded in Program.cs or appsettings.json. Administrators create them from the Administration > Rate Limiting screen, they are stored in the database, and they take effect at runtime without a restart or redeployment. This article explains how that feature works under the hood, how a request is matched to a policy, and how to design a policy set that protects the API without throttling legitimate users. It is written for developers, architects, and DevOps engineers who operate or extend Vineforce Teams, particularly in on-premise deployments. Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a time window, or how many it can have in flight at once. For a multi-tenant time-tracking platform it addresses four concrete risks: Credential attacks. Anonymous endpoints such as /api/TokenAuth/* are the first target for credential stuffing and password spraying. A per-IP limit makes large-scale guessing slow and noisy. Resource exhaustion. items.title: How to update one dynamic zone block in Strapi 5 (without deleting the others)
items.summary: You have a Strapi 5 page built from a dynamic zone: a hero, a feature grid and a call to action. You want to change the hero's heading and nothing else. So you send an update with the hero block, and the feature grid and the call to action are gone. That is how Strapi 5 writes lists. A dynamic zone, a repeatable component or a rich-text blocks field is replaced as a whole: the array you send becomes the new list, and anything you left out is deleted. The REST API works this way, and so does the update_ tool in Strapi's built-in MCP server. With one writer, that is a matter of sending the right array. With two writers, it is a race: each one sends a list built from its own read, the second write wins, and the first writer's block disappears with a 200 and no error. People keep running into this. One GitHub issue reads, "found that I cannot update component". A docs issue is blunter: "Updating dynamic zones via REST API does not work." It does work. It just doesn't work the way most of us assume the first time. Below are three routes, in order of how much control you have over the writer. items.title: Retrieval Architecture for Recruiting Candidate Search: Node.js Fallbacks Explained
items.summary: Recruiting search has two clocks: the candidate record changes now, while a web profile or policy page may be days old. Short answer: use staged retrieval with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that survives every fallback. For most property-management hiring teams, that means a tenant-scoped vector index first, a fresh web lookup second, and a deterministic “no answer” state instead of an unbounded crawl. Shape Invariant Best fit Main cost Central staged pipeline Every stage returns the same candidate, score, and source contract One team owns indexing and freshness More index jobs and metadata plumbing Federated fallback A source can be skipped without changing the answer schema Many teams own separate systems Harder ranking and observability I recommend the central staged pipeline when recruiting candidate search is the product. It keeps chunking and freshness decisions in one place. A federated design is reasonable when a company already runs Elasticsearch for resumes and a separate web search service for public context; forcing a migration creates more risk than it removes. items.title: EADDRINUSE address already in use: 4 safe fixes
items.summary: Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use means your Node.js server tried to open a port that another program is already using. Most of the time that "other program" is an old copy of your own server that never stopped. This guide shows how to find it on Windows, stop it safely, and make your app handle a busy port on its own. Every command below was run on Windows 11 with Node.js 26. A port is a numbered door on your computer, like 3000. Only one program can listen on a port at a time. When your server calls listen(3000) and something already owns port 3000, Node.js throws this error and your app stops: node:events:505 throw er; // Unhandled 'error' event ^ Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000 at Server.setupListenHandle [as _listen2] (node:net:2390:16) ... code: 'EADDRINUSE', errno: -4091, :::3000 is the IPv6 way of writing "every address, port 3000". The Node.js docs call EADDRINUSE "one of the most common errors raised when listening" (Node.js net docs). The usual causes, from most to least common: An old server is still running. items.title: Healthtech Shipment Webhook Deduplication: FIFO Queue Idempotency Key Beyond Five Minutes
items.summary: Short answer: use the FIFO queue's five-minute dedupe window to reduce a burst of repeated shipment events, but use a durable idempotency record and an outbox to decide whether a webhook delivery intent already exists. The queue can preserve ordering for a short interval; it cannot be the audit system for a healthtech notification that may be retried hours later. That is the distinction I want in an architecture decision record. A shipment update may need to fan out to many subscribers, while the sender, queue, worker, and receiver all have different retry boundaries. Exactly-once is a useful mindset for the database transition, not a promise that one HTTP request crossed several independent systems once. The producer should derive one stable idempotency key from the upstream event identity, such as shipment-8472:delivered:v3, and reuse it for every retry of that same business event. It should not generate a new key because a network response was late. The consumer should atomically compare that key and a payload digest with its durable event table before creating delivery intents for subscribers. items.title: TypeScript Contracts for React Email Tests
items.summary: Email tests become confusing when the UI, the test runner, and the delivery provider all speak different languages. A React component waits for a verification state, while a Node.js service waits for a message, and the test waits for both. When something is slow, the failure usually says only that a button never changed. The fix I like is a small TypeScript contract between the application and its mail test adapter. It makes the boundary explicit, gives every scenario a stable identity, and lets the same React test move from a fast fake transport to a real disposable mail address when the delivery path needs coverage. An email test is not just an assertion about a message. It is a short workflow: Create a scenario with a unique ID. Submit an address through the React form. Wait for the backend to send a message. Read the message and extract a link or code. Return to the UI and assert the next state. If each step exposes provider-specific details, the test becomes hard to read and harder to replace. items.title: Node.js Signed Download Links for Auditable Receipt Files Explained
items.summary: The safest Node.js export flow checks the player or operator's access before it creates a short-lived capability URL, while the original receipt stays immutable in private storage. That gives the client a simple download and keeps authorization in the application where tenant, role, and audit context are available. Short answer: treat a signed download URL as a delivery credential, not as an authorization system. Resolve an export record, verify access, sign the exact object key for a small time window, and log the decision without logging the URL itself. For a gaming receipt export, that separation matters: delivery should be easy, but a leaked link should have a narrow blast radius. The before model is familiar: the browser calls a public bucket path, and the application hopes the path is hard to guess. The after model has three steps: an authenticated request asks for an export, the application authorizes that request and signs one object, then the browser downloads directly from private storage. items.title: I made the database fail on purpose in a legacy checkout: /health stayed 200 and 3 of 214 specs turned red
items.summary: The complaint arrived as a screenshot: a spinner, then an error page, on a Tuesday afternoon. Three customers could not pay. By the time I opened the dashboard for that service, everything on it was green. Four instances up, CPU under 20%, uptime for the month a shade over 99.9%, no alert fired. The /health endpoint had answered 200 the whole time. Here is that endpoint, with the variable names changed: // routes/health.js router.get('/health', (req, res) => { res.status(200).json({ status: 'ok', version: pkg.version, uptime: process.uptime(), }) }) That endpoint cannot fail. It reads nothing and calls nothing, so it keeps answering 200 while Postgres refuses connections, which is exactly what it did for about 40 minutes. The service is around nine years old, roughly 40k lines of Node and Express, 214 specs in the suite, and a coverage badge in the README that reads 87%. The people who own it asked a fair question. The suite is green, coverage is high, so why did nothing catch this? Coverage answers how much code ran while the tests ran, not which failures anything in that repo can notice. I wanted the second answer before touching a single spec, and there is a cheap way to get it.

items.title: Private Image Originals and Thumbnails: Retention, Resizing, and Signed Downloads
items.summary: Short answer: use private object storage for originals and generated thumbnails, run resizing in your Node.js worker or an image service, and return short-lived signed download links. Choose a provider by its retention and recovery behavior, not by the existence of an image-resize checkbox. Infrai belongs in the shortlist when the team wants that storage workflow behind one REST contract. The decision still starts with retention and recovery. The storage bucket is the durable file cabinet. Your application owns authentication, thumbnail dimensions, and deletion policy. A worker reads an original, writes thumbs/{imageId}/{variant}.webp, and records width, height, and the object key in your database. The browser receives a signed URL only after the customer is authenticated. items.title: The Same Berlin Rent Search Priced the City at €11.51 and €33.63 per m . Only Page One Moved
items.summary: I run a visa agency in Bali. The other half of my week goes into Apify Actors, and one of them reads ImmoScout24 — Germany's biggest property portal. You give it a city, a district, a postcode or a pasted search URL; it gives you one row per listing with the rent as a number, €/m², living space, rooms, the full address with coordinates, energy class, the cost breakdown and the realtor. Because the Actor health-checks itself every night with the same prefilled example, I am not looking at a snapshot. I have a panel: 45 runs between 22 October and 17 November with byte-identical input — locations: ["Berlin"], propertyType: "apartmentrent", maxItems: 50, sortBy: "relevance", details on. 2,172 listing rows, 256 distinct apartments. (A forty-sixth run with the same input stopped at four rows; that one is a budget story, at the end.) Here is the thing that made me write this up. For each run I took the median of its 50 pricePerSqm values — the simplest possible "what does Berlin cost" number: run rows median €/m² 22 Oct 14:46 50 11.51 27 Oct 20:08 47 32.40 31 Oct 20:14 47 11.51 5 Nov 20:06 47 33.63 13 Nov 20:10 50 18.20 17 Nov 21:01 50 24.13 Same search. items.title: Valida la CURP con RENAPO y autocompleta la dirección por código postal en Node.js
items.summary: Casi todos los formularios de alta en México piden lo mismo: CURP, nombre, fecha de nacimiento y domicilio. Y casi todos fallan en lo mismo: La CURP "válida" que no existe. La regex la acepta, el dígito verificador cuadra, pero RENAPO no la tiene o pertenece a otra persona. La dirección escrita a mano. "Monterey", "N.L.", "Col. Centro" en un código postal que no tiene colonia Centro. Después nadie puede entregar el paquete ni cotejar el comprobante de domicilio. En este artículo armamos en Node.js (18 o más reciente, con fetch nativo) y Express un backend pequeño que resuelve las dos cosas: Revisa el formato de la CURP sin red (formato, fecha real, dígito verificador). La confirma con RENAPO y compara lo que la persona escribió contra lo que el registro tiene. Con los cinco dígitos del código postal llena estado, municipio y la lista de colonias del catálogo de Correos de México (SEPOMEX). Si la persona no sabe su código postal, lo busca por nombre de colonia. Para las consultas uso MexCheck, el API que construí (abajo va la aclaración completa). items.title: 'Java4Shell' Flaw Exposes OpenJDK to RCE via Base64
items.summary: Longtime Slashdot reader HnT writes: Security researchers at Calif have disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a critical 9.2-rated memory-corruption bug in OpenJDK's AVX-512 Base64 decoder. By sending a malformed string ending in a stray = character, attackers can trigger an out-of-bounds heap write to leak sensitive memory or achieve pre-auth remote code execution on major platforms like Jira, Jenkins, and Keycloak. Although Calif says the vulnerability is difficult to exploit, Oracle released a critical patch update Tuesday, and CISA urged organizations to update immediately. OpenJDK's security advisory can be found here. The Calif researchers warned that vulnerable systems could remain exposed for five to 10 years, given how slowly some organizations patch their infrastructure. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Cambridge Dictionary Names 'Human' Its 2026 Word of the Year
items.summary: Cambridge Dictionary has named "human" its 2026 Word of the Year, reflecting growing concerns about artificial intelligence and its impact on what it means to be human. "AI is changing how we talk about being human," said Colin McIntosh, the dictionary's lexicographer. "Fears about what humans may lose when we outsource our thinking have made us reconsider the extent to which we rely on AI: from top mathematicians to teachers of young children." The Associated Press reports: The adjective derived from the Latin "humanus" and in use since the 1450s is defined by Cambridge as "having the qualities, faults and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals or machines." [...] Other word contenders for 2026 included "agent," for an AI system that can make decisions and operate without human control and "analogue" for experiences or objects not involving the internet or digital technology. items.title: What gets rebuilt in a hundred merged changes
items.summary: Every design system has a gap between what it offers and what gets written. You can argue about that gap in the abstract for a long time. I wanted to look at it in real code, change by change, so I took a popular open-source document-sharing product and replayed its last hundred merged changes against the components and tokens it has today. This is what I found, how I checked it, and why the product stays anonymous. The idea is simple. Take a repository's recent history and, for each merged change, ask one question: did this change add something the codebase already had? For each change, the check looks only at the lines that change added, not the whole file it touched. It compares them with the components and design tokens the repository declares. Two kinds of finding count. Hand-built UI where a component already existed: a button element styled by hand where the codebase has Button, a pulsing grey block where it has a skeleton loader component. A raw value exactly equal to a token or scale step that already existed: a pixel size that is a step on the spacing scale, a colour that is the value of a declared colour token. items.summary: Hi HN, we're Ary and Maria, co-founders of Maritime (https://maritime.sh). We're building an agent-native cloud that handles everything from custom environments to lifecycle management for AI agents. Demo: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lCWMdBQ96rY There’s been an explosion of sandbox companies coming out of SF, but sandboxes solve maybe 10% of the infrastructure problem for AI agents. The approach that most sandboxing companies take is: You buy Hetzner/OVH Cloud bare metal servers, use Firecracker to slice the servers up into VMs, sell those VMs with low margins. It’s a bit of an oversimplification, but the point is it’s a narrow solution to a fairly difficult problem. We talked to a couple hundred companies that are building AI agents. From personal assistants and coding agents to specialized healthcare agents, and the main pattern we saw was that even after choosing a sandbox provider, you still have to build additional infrastructure just to get things working. items.summary: Introduction React is a popular JavaScript library used to build interactive user interfaces. One of its most powerful features is Hooks. Hooks allow functional components to use React features such as state management, side effects, and shared data without writing class components. Among the most commonly used React Hooks are: useState() useEffect() useContext() Let's understand each hook, how it works, and when to use it. useState() is a React Hook that allows us to create and manage state inside a functional component. State is data that can change over time. Whenever the state changes, React re-renders the component to display the updated information. const [state, setState] = useState(initialValue); state: Stores the current value. setState: Updates the state. initialValue: Defines the initial state. import React, { useState } from 'react'; function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ( Count: {count} setCount(count + 1)}> Increment setCount(count - 1)}> Decrement ); } export default Counter; Initially, the count value is 0. items.title: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google models readily marked medics, journalists, and surrendering soldiers as kamikaze drone targets

A realistic join curve: 25% of the bots join in the same moment, the way players do when the "show is live" push notification lands. items.title: A receipt that says "nothing was changed" has to be true
items.summary: Our Mac menu bar app has two buttons, Free Agent RAM and Stop Runaways. Each one runs a small Node.js script that finds agent processes eating memory or CPU, and stops them. When the script finishes, the app shows a receipt that lists what it did. If Node.js isn't installed, the script can't run. The app handles that: it shows "Couldn't free agent memory" and says what went wrong. Before the 1.2.10 release it also did something else first. It ran xcrun simctl shutdown all, which shuts down every simulator on the Mac. The order was the bug. In both button handlers, the call that shuts down simulators sat above the check for whether Node.js had run. A person without Node.js would click the button, see "Nothing was changed", and have every running simulator shut down anyway. The receipt was false. Nothing in the app could have told them otherwise, because the shutdown happened before the app looked at the result. The change was moving one line below the check. items.title: We Turned On Row-Level Security in Postgres. Four Things Broke.
items.summary: Row-level security looks like a one-line change in Postgres: create a policy, set a session variable, done. We turned it on for a multi-tenant commerce backend, and it took four fixes before it worked. Here they are, along with the decision we had to make. Every tenant-scoped table has a policy that compares its tenant_id to a session variable, app.tenant_id. The API sets that variable on each connection, from the authenticated user's tenant. A query that forgets its tenant filter gets no rows instead of another tenant's rows. That is the backstop we wanted. EF Core query filters already scope tenant reads for tenant-entity types, but a future handler that forgets the filter should fail closed, not leak. The app connects as a least-privilege role, not the superuser. Migrations run as a separate role. The interceptor resets the role and sets the tenant in a single command text. With a parameter in the same command, Npgsql's extended protocol rejects multiple statements. The fix was two calls instead of one. It is a small change, and it failed on the first real request. If you are a .NET team, that means a real inventory-and-replace job: NuGet packages, Stackify.json, log appenders, custom ProfileTracer operations, custom metrics, and (on Linux or in containers) the profiler GUID in environment variables. I built a small free tool for the inventory part. Retrace, the production APM, shuts down on 31 March 2027. Until then it is in maintenance mode: no new features, only critical fixes. Prefix, the local profiler, is not being switched off. Premium support and updates for Prefix end on the same date; BMC says Prefix premium features are already free. Prefix is not a production monitoring replacement. Exporting history is your job. Logs can be exported in files of up to 100,000 entries or 50 MB each. Custom dashboards can be saved as PDFs. items.title: .NET 11 chega com C# 15 e CoreCLR padrão no .NET MAUI
items.summary: .NET 11 chega com dois anos de suporte A Microsoft lançou o .NET 11 junto com C# 15, F# 11, ASP.NET Core 11, .NET MAUI e Entity Framework Core 11. A versão segue o modelo de suporte padrão (Standard Term Support, STS) e terá dois anos de manutenção; o .NET 10 permanece como opção de suporte de longo prazo. O lançamento coincidiu com a .NET Conf, realizada de 10 a 13 de novembro de 2026. No primeiro dia do evento, 10 de novembro, .NET 8 e .NET 9 chegaram ao fim do suporte. A mudança exige que equipes com aplicações nessas versões avaliem as opções de atualização disponíveis. C# 15 é a versão padrão para projetos direcionados ao .NET 11. A new screen shape is a rare chance to look good while most apps still look stretched or awkward. For a small indie app, being ready early is one of the few advantages I have over bigger teams. It also forced me to clean up assumptions I had been carrying around for years. No more hardcoded sizes. Anything that assumed "an iPhone is this wide" had to go. Adaptive layouts. Screens adjust to the space they get instead of assuming one fixed shape. Using the extra room well. On a bigger canvas, a family app can show more at once, like a shared calendar next to the details, without more taps. Testing in the simulator at different sizes, including the ones I hope are close to the real thing. If your layout only works on one screen size, you have a bug you haven't found yet. items.title: Inside swiftc: How Swift Turns Source into SIL, LLVM IR and Machine Code
items.summary: One small function followed through every stage of the Swift compiler, with real SIL, LLVM IR and x86-64 / ARM64 assembly, and a measured look at how optimization changes the cost of protocols, generics, closures and classes. Source → Lexer → Parser → AST → Type checker → SIL → SIL optimizer → LLVM IR → LLVM optimizer → Machine code → Object file → Linker → Binary Last year I lost most of an afternoon to a single line of arithmetic. It was in a geometry helper, nothing clever, a handful of numbers, a couple of Double(...) conversions and some parentheses. Every clean build took noticeably longer than it should have, and when I finally ran the compiler with type-checking timers switched on, that one line was the culprit. That sent me down a path I'd been avoiding for years: actually reading what swiftc produces between my source file and the binary. This article is the write-up I wish I'd had at the start. We'll follow one tiny function through every stage of the pipeline. We'll look at real SIL, real LLVM IR and real assembly. items.title: I shipped a habit app that only allows one habit
items.summary: Most habit apps become a second todo list. You add ten habits on day one, miss half of them on day two, and stop opening the app by day four. I shipped an iPhone app, bububaba, that refuses that loop. You start with one daily habit. Finish it, earn one water drop, and water a tree. The tree grows from sprout to sapling to mature, then you harvest fruit. Leave it too long and it wilts. A run of finished days brings it back. A second habit stays locked until you complete 30 days in a row. The app is free, English and Vietnamese, iOS 17 or later: bububaba on the App Store. I did not limit the app to one habit because the data model was hard. A list of habits is the easy version. The limit is there so the home screen can answer a single question: did I do the thing today? A Home Screen widget shows the task that is still waiting. The reminder fires at the time you choose, again near the end of the day, and when the tree is thirsty. Check-in is a tap, with an optional note and photo. That is the whole daily path. items.title: US Officially a Measles Endemic Country
items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from The Hill: The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) confirmed Tuesday that it was withdrawing the U.S.'s measles elimination status, ending more than two decades of what is considered to be one of the greatest public health achievements in modern history. The U.S. met with PAHO's Measles and Rubella Elimination Regional Monitoring and Re-Verification Commission for a three-day, closed-door meeting last week. "The commission concluded that the endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn, a recommendation which I have accepted," Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO's director, said during the briefing Tuesday. The U.S. achieved measles elimination status in 2000 and has held onto that for more than 25 years. But the past two years have seen close to 8,000 measles infections and roughly a dozen related deaths. This year has been the worst in terms of transmission in more than 30 years. items.title: Nvidia Rejects Jensen Huang's Offer to Return as CEO
items.summary: Nvidia's board has unanimously rejected former CEO Jensen Huang's offer to return, despite public support from President Trump and prominent Silicon Valley figures. The decision came as Nvidia reported blockbuster third-quarter revenue of $116 billion, double the year-earlier figure. The Associated Press reports: The embattled company's board of directors "unanimously accepted his resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO," Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones said at the start of Nvidia's quarterly earnings call before yielding to Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress, who is running the company as a permanent replacement is sought. [...] Earlier on Tuesday, Huang said in a social media post that if the board decided that his return was in the best interest of shareholders, employees, the company and the country, he would be "honored to answer these calls." He acknowledged making "serious mistakes" in his personal life. The turmoil notwithstanding, Nvidia blew past Wall Street expectations for the third quarter, pulling in $116 billion in revenue, double the level from a year ago. The company also posted net income of $2.70 per share, beating estimates of $2.48 per share.

items.title: Muting the mic for every app on macOS with Core Audio
items.summary: Zoom, Teams and Meet each have their own mute, and they don't know about each other. I wanted one hotkey that mutes the mic for everything, so I made a small menu bar app for it. It sets kAudioDevicePropertyMute on the input devices through Core Audio, so every app just gets silence. By default it mutes all inputs, not only the default one, because Zoom and Meet often disagree about which mic is "the" mic. It also listens for changes and puts the mute back if some app flips it. ⌘⇧M toggles it, and there's push to talk too. Later I added optional local recording of the mic plus system audio into one small file, which is handy for dropping a call into ChatGPT or Claude for a summary. It's free and MIT, macOS 14+: github.com/oochernyshev/lockmic. I'm the developer, happy to answer Core Audio questions.

items.title: How to check a license key in your Mac app offline
items.summary: Short answer: Sign each license on your server with Ed25519, then verify it in the app with CryptoKit and the matching public key. Honest customers stay unlocked offline, because the check does not need a network call. Verify the signature and the expiry at launch and again where the paid feature runs, not in a single isLicensed() flag. A shared serial list, or a secret compiled into the app, can be copied out of the binary. Anyone who has that secret can invent keys your app will accept, or share one serial widely. AI tools make that read faster than it used to be. A signed license works the other way around. Your server holds a private key and signs a small payload: the customer's email, the product name, and an expiry. The app ships the public key and uses it to verify the signature. The public key cannot issue a new license. Sign the raw payload bytes. Then ship the payload and the signature as standard Base64, joined by a period: base64(payload) + "." + base64(signature) The payload is JSON, for example: {"email":"customer@example.com","product":"MyApp","expiry":"2027-11-17T00:00:00Z"} Leave the payload machine-agnostic unless you have a clear reason to bind a device, so the s

items.title: How InkHammy checks grammar in every Mac app with the Accessibility API
items.summary: I'm Zak, and I build InkHammy, a grammar checker that runs as a Mac menu bar app and as an iPhone keyboard. Disclosure up front: InkHammy is my product. This post isn't a review; it's a write-up of how the Mac app reads and fixes text inside other apps through the macOS Accessibility API, and the design choices that came out of it. A browser extension only sees web pages. A lot of writing on a Mac happens somewhere else: Slack, Mail, Notes, Messages, the ChatGPT app, and text fields inside desktop apps built on web views. To check text in all of them, an app has to follow whichever field has focus, read its text, know where each word sits on screen, and write corrections back without breaking the host app. macOS exposes this through the Accessibility API (AX). The user grants Accessibility permission once in System Settings, and the app can then observe and act on UI elements in other processes. AX is powerful, but every host app implements it a little differently, and a call into a busy app can block. Most of InkHammy's Mac architecture exists to deal with those two facts. items.title: Why I took Whisper out of my iPhone transcription app before it shipped
items.summary: I work on Koedori at W Lab. It is an iPhone app that records a lecture, a meeting or an interview and turns it into text on the phone itself, with no account, and the audio is never uploaded. The early builds ran Whisper through WhisperKit. The version on the App Store has no Whisper in it at all: it uses Apple's SpeechAnalyzer framework and its SpeechTranscriber module. This post is about why, and what building on SpeechTranscriber is like. Koedori makes three promises: transcription is free and needs no account, audio never leaves the phone, and re-transcribing costs nothing, as often as you like. The second one is architecture, not a setting. There is no code path that uploads audio, and the app has no server of its own. So recognition has to run on the device, and it has to be cheap enough to run again on a whim. Whisper on the phone met that on paper. The trouble was everything around the model. WhisperKit compiles a model for the Neural Engine the first time it loads it. On the iPhone 14 I measured, the first load of large-v3 turbo after an install took 197 to 205 seconds, every time. items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. That means that (a+b)+c is not always equal to a+(b+c). This post looks at what happens when integer addition, which is exact, is used.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.
